n0001.title: Cargo Cult Science
n0001.gist: Science that copies the form of real science but skips rigorous self-doubt looks right yet never actually works.
n0001.question: Cargo Cult Science — what separates real science from its hollow imitation?

n0002.title: Opening Remarks
n0002.gist: A commencement speech introduces its subject: why fields that mimic science's outward form can still fail to produce real, working results.
n0002.question: Cargo Cult Science — what is this talk actually about? (a thesis statement)

n0003.title: Title and author
n0003.gist: The talk's title, reading time, and speaker.

n0007.title: Opening thesis
n0007.gist: The talk promises remarks on science, pseudoscience, and how to avoid fooling yourself, delivered as Caltech's 1974 commencement address.

n0009.title: Hunting for Pseudoscience
n0009.gist: Feynman surveys mysticism, ESP, education, and criminal justice, finding fields that look scientific yet never improve, which he names Cargo Cult Science.
n0009.question: pseudoscience — what do mysticism, education, and crime policy share that marks them as fake science? (several examples)

n0010.title: Scientific method emerges
n0010.gist: Medieval superstitions gave way to science once people learned to test an idea by trying it and discarding it if it failed to work.

n0012.title: Modern mysticism investigated
n0012.gist: Feynman investigates UFOs, isolation tanks, and Esalen's mystic culture, becoming overwhelmed by how much unproven belief still thrives in a supposedly scientific age.

n0015.title: Massage session anecdote
n0015.gist: A bathhouse anecdote about a man pretending to locate the pituitary gland through foot massage mocks pseudoscientific jargon dressed up as expertise.

n0017.title: Uri Geller demonstration
n0017.gist: Feynman attends a demonstration by Uri Geller, supposedly able to bend keys and read minds, but witnesses no effect under any tested condition.

n0019.title: Failures in education and crime policy
n0019.gist: Reading scores and crime rates fail to improve despite elaborate theories, suggesting these fields resemble witch-doctor remedies dressed as science.

n0023.title: Cocktail party test
n0023.gist: Feynman proposes a joking rule: if a topic can be discussed endlessly at a party without seeming like shop talk, nobody really understands it.

n0025.title: Psychotherapy studies
n0025.gist: Using his cocktail-party test, Feynman adds psychotherapy's effectiveness to his growing list of widely believed but poorly tested subjects.

n0027.title: Cargo Cult Science named
n0027.gist: Feynman compares these pseudosciences to Pacific islanders who rebuild runways and control towers hoping planes will land, calling such empty imitation Cargo Cult Science.

n0029.title: The Principle of Scientific Integrity
n0029.gist: Real science demands leaning over backward to report every flaw and contrary fact, not merely the evidence that favors your own theory.
n0029.question: scientific integrity — what exactly must a scientist disclose to be honest? (a definition with examples)

n0030.title: Reporting all relevant details
n0030.gist: Feynman defines the missing ingredient in cargo cult science as a leaning-over-backward honesty: reporting everything that might invalidate your own result.

n0032.title: Disclosing disagreeing facts
n0032.gist: A theory must be presented alongside every fact that disagrees with it, and its fit must be tested against data beyond what inspired it.

n0034.title: Summary of integrity idea
n0034.gist: The goal is giving others all the information needed to judge your work's value, not only the evidence pointing one direction.

n0036.title: Contrast with advertising
n0036.gist: An oil advertisement's technically true claim that it doesn't soak through food misleads by implication, showing scientific integrity requires more than avoiding outright lies.

n0038.title: Truth will out
n0038.gist: Because other experimenters and nature itself will eventually reveal errors, a scientist's reputation depends on having been careful and honest from the start.

n0040.title: Difficulty of the subject
n0040.gist: Some fields are simply hard to study scientifically, but Feynman insists that difficulty alone does not explain why their methods keep failing.

n0042.title: Lessons in Self-Deception
n0042.gist: Historical and political examples—from Millikan's drifting measurements to selective publication—show how bias creeps in unless inconvenient results get reported too.
n0042.question: self-deception — how do scientists and advisors quietly let bias shape what gets published? (several case examples)

n0043.title: Millikan's electron charge drift
n0043.gist: Millikan's early measurement of the electron's charge was slightly wrong, and later values crept upward slowly instead of jumping straight to the correct number.

n0045.title: Why errors went unnoticed
n0045.gist: Scientists unconsciously hunted harder for flaws in results that strayed far from Millikan's number, letting a wrong value persist long after better data existed.

n0047.title: Lesson learned, still untaught
n0047.gist: This history of self-deception is never formally taught in any course, leaving students to absorb scientific integrity only by informal example.

n0049.title: First principle: don't fool yourself
n0049.gist: The foremost rule of scientific integrity is guarding against fooling yourself first, since that is easier than any other kind of dishonesty to fall into.

n0051.title: Integrity toward laymen
n0051.gist: Feynman extends scientific honesty beyond fellow scientists, arguing researchers also owe ordinary people a truthful account of their work when speaking publicly.

n0053.title: Cosmologist's dishonest justification
n0053.gist: A colleague wanted to invent practical applications for his astronomy research just to secure funding, which Feynman condemns as a failure of honesty toward the public.

n0055.title: Publish regardless of outcome
n0055.gist: Results must be published whichever way they come out, since selectively publishing favorable findings—as cigarette companies do—distorts the truth for the audience.

n0057.title: Scientific advice to politicians
n0057.gist: Advice to politicians is not truly scientific if unfavorable findings are suppressed while convenient ones are publicized, turning expertise into a tool of persuasion.

n0059.title: Failures to Replicate
n0059.gist: A psychology student and a physics lab both skip repeating a baseline experiment before changing conditions, a shortcut that quietly undermines scientific conclusions.
n0059.question: replication — why does skipping a baseline experiment ruin a result's reliability? (two case studies)

n0060.title: Rat experiment proposal at Cornell
n0060.gist: A psychology student wanted to test whether rats would still behave the same way under new conditions, without first repeating the original experiment herself.

n0062.title: Need to replicate baseline first
n0062.gist: Feynman advises the student to first reproduce the original result under the old conditions, so she can be sure any later change is truly responsible for a difference.

n0064.title: Professor blocks replication
n0064.gist: Her professor forbade repeating the earlier experiment as wasted time, reflecting a 1930s norm against replication in psychology research.

n0066.title: Accelerator experiment shortcut
n0066.gist: A physicist at a major accelerator reused mismatched old data instead of rerunning a comparison experiment, pressured by limited machine time and a push for new results.

n0068.title: Young's Rat Experiment
n0068.gist: One meticulous rat study uncovers the true cues animals use, yet later researchers ignore it, the same neglect that lets unrepeatable ESP claims persist.
n0068.question: Young's experiment — why does careful work get ignored while sloppy science persists? (a case study and a counterexample)

n0069.title: Young's door experiment
n0069.gist: In 1937, Young tried training rats to choose a specific door in a corridor, but they kept returning to wherever food had been before instead.

n0071.title: Eliminating sensory clues
n0071.gist: Young systematically ruled out visual texture, smell, and lighting as the cues rats used to recognize the correct door, yet the rats still succeeded.

n0073.title: Sound in the floor
n0073.gist: Young discovered rats were detecting floor sound, which he eliminated only by running the corridor over sand, finally forcing true learning of the task.

n0075.title: An exemplary experiment
n0075.gist: Young's painstaking elimination of every possible clue makes his study a model for how to control conditions properly in any rat-running experiment.

n0077.title: Ignored by later researchers
n0077.gist: Despite its rigor, Young's work and his sand-corridor method were never cited by later rat researchers, who kept making the same uncontrolled mistakes.

n0079.title: Rhine's shrinking ESP effects
n0079.gist: As parapsychologists refine their techniques under criticism, the measured ESP effects shrink toward nothing, yet researchers still resist demanding a repeatable experiment.

n0081.title: Parapsychology institute's policy
n0081.gist: A retiring parapsychology director advised training only students who already get positive results, a policy that teaches getting an answer rather than doing honest science.

n0083.title: Closing Wish
n0083.gist: Feynman closes by wishing graduates the freedom to keep scientific integrity despite institutional or financial pressure to abandon it.
n0083.question: closing wish — what does Feynman hope for the graduates? (a benediction)
